title: Medibank boss cracks open a can of worms
full_text:
Medibank Private chief executive David Koczkar has a meerkat in his bonnet.
Lobbing reporting season's first big grenade, Koczkar accused insurance aggregators, which most of us know as the online comparison sites such as Compare The Market and its sister brand iSelect, of doing little more than encouraging churn, driving up premiums and adding $200 million in costs to a sector where every dollar is supposed to be closely scrutinised.
Koczkar made the comments on Thursday's earnings call and was happy to double down afterwards. He said the aggregators charged "opaque" commissions worth up to 30 per cent of the first year of a premium, customers didn't understand how they worked, three-quarters of their business was shuffling customers between funds rather than growing the sector, and the only true source of comparison across all funds is a government-run service most people have probably never heard of.
"Every cost in private health needs to be held to the same standard," he says. "The risk is that the industry spends more money on the sales and that puts more pressure on the premiums." He told analysts these aggregators had increased sales 44 per cent in the past two years, a period that coincides with the return of cost-of-living pressures, and the industry's commissions paid had almost doubled. Had customers benefited? Medibank premiums increased by 5.1 per cent on average on April 1 and 4 per cent last year.
It is interesting because Koczkar's Medibank continues to use some (not all) of these aggregators to sell policies for its cheap-and-cheerful No.2 brand ahm, and they were ahm's best new business driver for years. It cut ties with one of the big aggregators in December, but still spent $70 million on aggregator commissions in FY26, down from about $80 million a year earlier. They're a bit of a dirty little secret.
So he's a user, just not as much as he used to be. What he's asking is that this part of the private health insurance cost chain is held to the same scrutiny as everything else - such as private hospital costs or medical devices.
It was quite the broadside from a chief executive who consistently talked down private health's scrap with the insurers last year, and investors wondered whether he was trying to deflect from a result that was otherwise pretty poorly received. He mentioned the same aggregator cause at the Macquarie Australia investor conference in May and followed it up with some choice words on Thursday.
CEOs are backgrounding about rivals or third-party suppliers such as aggregators all the time, but they rarely do it in public.
It came as Medibank's FY26 numbers were in line with expectations. However, its FY27 guidance was a bit soft and the stock was down 9 per cent in afternoon trading. Investors are worried about downgrading - Medibank customers switching to cheaper or lower-value products, also a factor for other dominant Australian consumer-facing businesses such as Telstra and JB Hi-Fi. Medibank chief financial officer Mark Rogers called that out in Thursday morning's chat with analysts.
But Koczkar says this is an important discussion to be had. He has scaled back Medibank's use of aggregators (19 per cent of new customers in the past six months versus 26 per cent at the same time last year) to try to put some of his money where his mouth is.
"They [aggregators] play a role but the cost has been growing in plain sight," he says.
The biggest aggregators include Compare the Market and iSelect, both owned by Innovation Holdings Australia, part of a bigger family of companies that also includes general insurance underwriter Budget Direct. Innovation Holdings owned Compare the Market and bought iSelect in 2022.
ANTHONY MACDONALD
Fairfax Media Management Pty Limited
